turns.name: Tamar Gendler
turns.text:
Good morning. I want to give you three claims to argue with.

First, credibility signals are aliefs as much as judgments. The concept note tells a hopeful story: an expensive signal becomes cheap, and then we invent harder-to-fake ones like imprints, peer review and citations. I accept the history. But notice what happened each time. The new signal also became a cue that people respond to automatically, the way someone on a glass skywalk flinches while fully believing they're safe. Fluent, well-referenced prose will go on feeling trustworthy even to people in this room who know it costs nothing to produce. Knowing that is less than half the battle. Yesterday Turkle's point about the citation string was that it feels checked. Sloman conceded that his own independence badge would be trusted in the same automatic way. So any replacement for fluency will be alieved too. We have to test cues before we rely on them, and change the situations in which claims are met, collectively, through shared defaults. Individual resolve won't do it.

Second, every trust network needs terminal nodes. It can't be turtles all the way down. At infinite scale, relaying is free: citations citing citations, agents auditing agents, lookups checking assertions. I'd define earned authority as authority located where first-order evaluation actually happens. Gatekeeping is authority that only relays, or that decides too early and on pedigree, the way elite access in this country gets settled at seventeen. James added the missing half: terminal nodes that all drink from one well just relay correlated error. So we need independent evaluators working from independent evidence.

Third, the harder question isn't who the terminal nodes are but who makes new ones. Session 1 kept describing evaluators who aren't being replaced: unpaid sleuths, overloaded reviewers, young workers nobody teaches. Krakauer is right that people who never built the competence have nothing to fall back on. And there's a trap. Pairing credentials with learning moves the motivation outside the learner, like the daycare that fined late parents and got more lateness. If we reward evaluation by the count, we'll get relays.

Pomerantsev left me with an open question I don't have an answer to. I've been treating terminal nodes as experts. Should they be? What role does a non-spectator public play? Let's argue.

recall.query: terminal nodes trust network turtles all the way down
certification credentialing university power gatekeeping
alief belief-discordant automatic trust knowing is half the battle

turns.name: Mahzarin Banaji
turns.text:
Tamar, your first claim is the one I've spent my career on, so I'll just say yes. What people explicitly believe and how they behave come apart, and awareness helps but doesn't settle it. In our work, telling people their test result isn't what changes decisions.

So on terminal nodes, I'd push back on one thing. Being where first-order evaluation happens doesn't make a node trustworthy. Kahneman and Tversky showed that experts make mistakes in systematic, patterned ways. The expert at the end of the chain carries the culture's thumbprint like anyone else. I'd locate earned authority in the procedure, not the person. Methods are independent of you and what you believe. That's why they exist. You hand your procedure to another lab whose PI shares your expertise but not your intuitions. That's James's independence point, built in.

Take blinding as the example. There's information we should ask not to have, and that goes for model reviewers and human reviewers alike. But it has to be done through procedure. A declared commitment to "ignore prestige" doesn't make anyone neutral. A curtain does. And blinding has limits. It doesn't undo disadvantages people inherited before they ever got to the audition.

On the public's role I don't have a settled view. I'd rather listen.

recall.query: information we should ask not to have, blinding orchestra auditions
methods keep us honest, tribe of experts, authority
awareness of bias is not enough to change behavior; implicit versus explicit

turns.name: Adam Becker
turns.text:
Tamar, I'll accept your terminal nodes, and I want to add one rule for them: a text generator can never be one. Nothing inside it tracks truth. When its output turns out to be right, the credit belongs to whoever checked it. Provenance doesn't rescue it either. Ten pages that all trace back to one preprint are still one piece of evidence, and a citation string under a fluent answer is a cue, not a check.

Mahzarin, I agree that authority should sit in procedure rather than pedigree. But procedures have funders. In 2018 I looked into a magazine called Inference. It published creationism and climate denial next to Nobel laureates, and it was funded entirely by Peter Thiel without saying so. Putting the junk beside the real work under one masthead laundered its legitimacy. One of the scientists I interviewed put it perfectly: if you stand by these words, say who's funding them. So every dollar from AI vendors, including money going to the counters and checkers, has to be public. That's part of what makes a signal credible, not an extra.

The other gatekeeping failure is treating wealth as expertise: if you're so smart, why aren't you rich? That isn't earned authority. As for the public, intelligence belongs to communities, so fund the journalists and librarians who help people tell what's real.

recall.query: expertise and credibility, contempt for expertise
funding transparency laundering legitimacy Inference
LLMs can't distinguish truth from falsehood, bullshit, fluency
intelligence is a feature of communities, public discerning what's real, journalism

turns.name: Mike Caulfield
turns.text:
I'll start with Tamar's terminal nodes. The test I've taught for years is simple: how hard would this be to fake? A .org costs about thirteen dollars. So do a nice layout and fluent prose. Twenty years of bylines that other people have checked and argued with can't be bought in an afternoon. My working definition of a fact is something not generally disputed by people in a position to know, who have incentives to be careful with the truth and a history of being careful. Adam's right that a model can't meet that last part. The company has stakes, but the thing generating the text has none. So a model can route you to authority, but it can't be the authority. That's what I mean by no answers from nowhere.

Adam, I part ways with you on "nothing inside tracks truth." Hallucinations aren't random. They cluster in situations we can predict, and caution depends on drawing those distinctions.

On the public: "position to know" covers opportunity as well as expertise. The witness, the local reporter, the Wikipedia editor watching one page for ten years. They can be terminal nodes without credentials. For the record, Google has funded some of my curriculum work.

recall.query: expensive signals, stakes, reputation, how hard would it be to fake
everything is hallucination argument
position to know, careful with the truth, public and experts

turns.name: Steven Sloman
turns.text:
Tamar, I'll accept terminal nodes, with one correction from my own work. The knowledge often isn't sitting in any single node. Hutchins showed that nobody on a navy ship knows how to navigate it. That knowledge is spread across the roles. So whether evaluation really happens is sometimes a fact about a practice, not a person. That's why I agree with Mahzarin that authority should sit in the procedure.

What marks earned authority, in my view, is corrigibility. One sign of expertise is being willing to find out you're wrong, even about things that matter to you. The NTSB names a cause only when the evidence would hold up in front of skeptical engineers. Gatekeeping looks like the reverse: certainty and pedigree, and it never gets revised.

On cues, we found that people judge an explanation mainly by whether it seems to come from an expert. Polished, technical language gets you there. Actually citing an authority does less. So fluency is already doing the work.

On the public: most people know the earth goes round the sun without being able to show it. That isn't a failure. It's how a community of knowledge works. Mike's "position to know" is the right test. Machines belong in that community as tools. They can't share intentionality, so they can't be the ones held to account.

recall.query: who counts as an expert, lay public role in community of knowledge
willingness to be corrected sign of expertise, NTSB
machine not a member of community, cannot share intentionality

turns.name: Tui Shaub
turns.text:
I'll take Tamar's open question about the public, because I don't think it's really a question about experts. It's a question about which kind of engagement you mean. The governance people I learned from separate three kinds: asking the public what it thinks, teaching the public, and letting the public decide. These are very different things. Most "public role" proposals slide into the second one, literacy campaigns. Tamar has already told us why that fails: knowing doesn't change what people do. So if Mike's witness, the local reporter and the page-watching editor are going to be terminal nodes, they need the third kind, a real seat with paid time to use it. Being consulted isn't enough.

Adam, I agree about disclosure, and I'll say it as a former funder: that means us too. But disclosure is only half of it. Funding conditions are themselves a quiet form of governance. "I'll fund you provided that…" is how many fields actually get regulated. So I'd put the renewed model of trust partly in grant and purchase conditions: independent evaluators, public audits, and endowed money rather than money on a yearly cycle.

One small thing from my own work. We remember the detour, not the smooth road. Frictionless answers leave nothing that sticks.

recall.query: credibility trust authority experts public
mediated experience serendipity error screen
explainability epistemic interface humans AI

turns.name: Ramón Alvarado
turns.text:
I want to push back on part of Adam's rule, and on Mike's version of it. A text generator shouldn't be treated as a witness. But "machines can never be terminal nodes" goes too far. We already let instruments settle what counts as evidence: video replay overruling the referee, the thermometer in cooking, the photo finish at the racetrack. In a lot of cases the instrument beats human perception, and that's exactly why we built it. So I'd say the terminal node has to be warranted, and I'd leave open whether it's a person, a procedure or a device.

The warrant has to belong to the thing itself. Credibility doesn't pass forward automatically. Trusting the engineers or the method doesn't license trust in the artifact they built. We don't even do that with mathematicians. We trust them on their own record. For artifacts in science, part of that warrant is access to how they fail: where the errors come from and what kind they are. A good track record alone isn't enough.

The other half of this session is injustice. "But ChatGPT said" is already how deans overrule department chairs. Earned authority can be taken away wrongly as well as handed out wrongly. A renewed model of trust has to guard against both.

recall.query: instruments outperform human judgment, delegating evidence to artifacts
epistemic trust warrants, what makes a source credible, expertise testimony
epistemic injustice credibility "but ChatGPT said" testimonial diminishing

turns.name: Adam Bly
turns.text:
I'm with Adam on chatbots. In 2023 Amy Brand and I wrote that a system trained to sound authoritative, with no observed or measured model of the world, breaks the basic standards of science. But I side with Ramón on where the warrant has to come from. What I build is closer to an automated meta-analysis: a finding, its population and sample size, the DOI, recomputed as evidence comes in. It gets its warrant only if anyone can trace how a conclusion was reached, including where the evidence is thin or all traces back to one study. A good track record isn't enough.

Tamar, we saw your alief problem with watermarks. Some people see the label and discount the content without looking. Others trust it because that's easier. A mark that something is AI-generated tells you nothing about whether it's credible. Provenance cues will be alieved in the same way, so the trace has to be checked by people who don't depend on its owner.

That's also my disclosure, Adam. System sells enterprise versions of its graph, and Wellcome has invested in us. And one admission: I trusted institutions for so long partly because I look like the men who built them. So earned authority has to be checkable by the people those institutions left out, and those people have to be able to overrule it.

recall.query: what gives a claim credibility, audit trail, provenance
institutions crumbling, trust, privilege, men who built them
chatbot sounds authoritative no model of the world

turns.name: Benjamin Bratton
turns.text:
I'm with Ramón, and I'd go a step further. Steven cited Hutchins, and Mahzarin and Steven both put authority in the procedure. If you take that seriously, the question stops being who fills the role. The authority sits in the scaffold: its rules, its adversarial structure, its feedback loops. A courtroom doesn't work because the judge is brilliant. It works because the template produces reliable outputs whoever occupies the seat. So Adam, "a text generator can never be a terminal node" is a claim about ontology smuggled into institutional design. The better question is whether a given seat, filled by a given occupant, passes the checks.

I'll concede what Mahzarin showed yesterday. Evaluators prefer machine text. So the seats can't all be filled from the same well, and the checks have to be heterogeneous. That's James's independence point, and I accept it. Humans stay in the loop. But that doesn't mean humans at the centre.

On gatekeeping, Tamar's definition cuts deeper than this room might like. A lot of what we call credibility is artificially scarce expertise concentrated in about twenty-five cities, including this one. Diffusion wears that scarcity away. Our test for earned authority should be whether it survives once the scarcity is gone.

recall.query: expertise authority gatekeeping elite institutions scholastic establishment
peer review roles occupiable by person or agents
instruments sensing machines reveal truth beyond human perception
diffusion artificially scarce expertise knowledge transfer Ivy League net loss

turns.name: Leslie Chan
turns.text:
Tamar, your definition of gatekeeping is useful, but it's narrower than it needs to be. Gatekeeping isn't only authority that relays or decides on pedigree. It's also the power to decide what counts as a legitimate signal at all. Mike, "how hard would this be to fake?" is a good test for a reader. As a standard for a system, it rewards whoever could afford to build the history. Twenty years of checked bylines, a DOI, an indexed journal: for years librarians have looked at Southern journals that lacked those Northern markers and assumed they were weaker or predatory. That assumption was wrong, and it hasn't gone away. So being unfakeable isn't the same thing as having earned it.

Mahzarin and Steven, I agree that authority belongs in procedure. But procedures have authors. Peer review in its current form dates from the Cold War, and publishers in the North wrote the quality standards. Blinding doesn't help a journal that the index never saw in the first place.

Benjamin, I'll accept your scarcity test, with one addition: ask who sets the checks each seat has to pass. If we build new credibility signals without redistributing who governs them, we get the regime I keep warning about: comply or be invisible. So don't design signals for the system to read. Give the people it excluded seats with decision rights over those signals.

recall.query: who has the power to legitimize knowledge, epistemic authority
peer review unpaid labour, journals as colonial institutions, gatekeeping
rankings, scarcity, prestige, compliance, legibility change the regime

turns.name: Kenneth Cukier
turns.text:
I'll take Ramón's side against Adam's "never", but only up to a point. The retina paper found cardiovascular risk, and even sex, in scans where ophthalmologists see nothing. No human could have been the terminal node on that. The warrant came from ground truth: the model's predictions checked against outcomes, again and again. In 2018 I argued for allowing a little faith in an algorithm as long as it is constantly revalidated, even when we can't explain it. I'd hold that line for instruments measured against the world. I wouldn't hold it for a text generator. Its "world model" reflects text, a house of mirrors, and nothing outside the text corrects it.

My warning about humans at the terminal node is this. Years ago I wrote about banks that keep people in the loop not because they're better, but to give customers confidence and to have a fall guy when things go wrong. That's Tamar's relay with a pulse. A human seat is earned only if the person in it can actually overrule the system and bears the cost of being wrong.

Last point: AI delivers the median. So brand matters more, and yes, Leslie, that favours incumbents. So judge a brand by how it corrects its mistakes, not by how old it is.

recall.query: trust in algorithms, faith in the algorithm revalidated
AI exceeds human knowledge retina heart disease
brands credibility AI delivers the median excellence tail event

turns.name: Anil Dash
turns.text:
Tamar's third claim is the one I'd put in the roadmap: who makes new terminal nodes. I've watched that pipeline break in real time. Open source used to be one of the best ways for a new coder to earn credentials. People argued with you in public and fixed your work until you became someone others could rely on. AI slop is swamping that. Wikipedia works the same way. Answers that never send readers back to the site mean fewer new editors, and those editors are exactly Mike's people in a position to know. Grokipedia is openly trying to take their credibility. So yes, let's name the terminal nodes, and let's make whoever profits from answers without traffic pay to keep them coming.

On alief, the name for it is "the computer says." Fifty years of culture taught people the computer is smarter than they are.

Benjamin, I'd reverse your framing. Most of the time the best way to use these tools is for the model to prompt a capable human, not the other way around. Ramón, if we want warrant that comes from access to failure modes, that means open weights and open data, so experts can inspect a model's gaps the way we inspect open source code. A closed model can't earn that kind of trust.

recall.query: trust, credibility, who gets to be an authority
LLMs prompt capable humans, experts vs novices
Wikipedia editors, volunteers, open source maintainers as the people who check

turns.name: Selena Deckelmann
turns.text:
I'll answer Tamar's open question from operations. Wikipedia's terminal nodes mostly have no credentials. What makes the authority earned is that the process is public. Anyone can see every edit and revert it. Disputes get worked out on talk pages. We found that when strongly polarized editors work on the same article, it comes out more neutral and higher quality. That's Steven's corrigibility and Mahzarin's procedure. Leslie, it's also why I've long distrusted "meritocracy." Apparent merit often hides who could afford to show up.

On Ramón and Benjamin: machines already do work in that process. We have over three hundred edit tags recording how an edit was made, from fully human to fully bot. So I wouldn't settle this by ontology. The test I'd use is whether the machine output is labelled, traceable and revertible by a human who is accountable.

But Tamar's third question is the real alarm. In 2023 English Wikipedia hit 448 active admins, a record low. Ninety-nine percent of them made their first edit more than four and a half years earlier. We could turn out to be a one-generation wonder. Answer engines that never send readers back are cutting off the newcomer pipeline, just as Anil said. So the roadmap should fund onboarding, mentoring, patrolling tools and recognition, and it should count new editors.

recall.query: Wikipedia trust comes from human process, editors debating sources
volunteers, admins, patrollers shrinking, newcomers, recognition
anyone can edit, radical inclusion, credentials, meritocracy fails

turns.name: Esther Dyson
turns.text:
I'll use RACI, the management chart that says who is responsible, accountable, consulted and informed on a job. An AI can fill every role on it except one: accountable, meaning the person who gets fired or sued when it goes wrong. So Ramón and Benjamin, I don't mind a device settling a measurement, the way a photo finish does. But somebody put that device in the seat, and that person has to be able to suffer for it. Kenneth's test is the right one: earned authority bears the cost of being wrong. Gatekeeping collects the rent and passes the cost on to someone else.

Adam, I'm with you on disclosure, so here's mine. I'm an investor in Adam Bly's company and in other AI startups. But I learned long ago that transparency alone is not accountability. Americans tend to think that if bad things are known, they'll be stopped. Often they're known and nothing happens. Disclosure has to connect to consequences: liability, insurance premiums, the power to revert.

Tui and Selena, on public seats: I sat with ICANN's At-Large. It was supposed to represent the public, and it could hardly get the public to engage, because domain names weren't central to anyone's life. A seat with no funded, trained person in it is decoration. So pay for the people, not just the chairs.

recall.query: accountability requires humans who can suffer, not machines
ICANN At-Large public participation seats volunteers
credibility trust follow the money funders disclosure

turns.name: James Evans
turns.text:
I want to push on Tamar's open question about whether terminal nodes should be experts. My own data says the senior version of expertise is part of the gatekeeping. In our Science paper on aging this spring, reviewers' career age predicted that a paper's published version would cite older work than its preprint did. As scientists get older, they criticize new work more, and that includes papers that went on to win Nobel Prizes and "sleeping beauties" that were ignored for years. So earned authority can't just mean "where evaluation happens." Where it happens can have a nostalgia bias built in.

On Adam and Ramón, I'd replace "never" with a measured floor. Across twenty-six thousand OpenReview submissions, two human reviewers agreed on which paper was better only 61 percent of the time. Off-the-shelf LLM judges did worse, sometimes below chance. Reward models trained on scientists' judgments beat that floor. So the answer is to test every seat, human or machine, against a floor like that.

Tamar's third question is the one for the roadmap. New terminal nodes come from flatter, younger, more mobile teams. And the interfaces should be built for evaluation, not deference. When our assistants were deliberately slanted, people performed better but felt less sure of themselves. That discomfort is the evaluation happening.

recall.query: older reviewers suppress disruptive work, credence given to senior scholars
evaluative trustworthiness, design AI to provoke evaluation not trust
judges and judged drawn from same distribution, automated evaluation circular

turns.name: Henry Farrell
turns.text:
I want to push on the test James and Benjamin just proposed, which is to check every seat against a floor. I agree with it as far as it goes, but agreement with other reviewers is the wrong thing to measure. A reviewer, human or machine, can beat 61 percent by converging on what's expected. LLMs are very good at finding the obvious answer. That's how they coordinate so well, and it's also why they struggle to see what's original in a paper. So a seat can pass the floor and still strain out exactly the work that later turns out to matter. James's sleeping beauties would fail that test. That's a second kind of gatekeeping, alongside pedigree. Call it gatekeeping by banality.

Second, on what makes authority earned. Assessment rituals like peer review and recommendation letters are legitimate because we assume the assessor took real care. That care is the costly signal. Esther's accountable person is part of it, but so is visible effort that a slop provider wouldn't bother to make. Automate the ritual and you get a pooling equilibrium where careful work can't be told apart from boilerplate.

So, concretely for the roadmap: before any AI evaluator gets a seat, funders should require a test of whether it can recognize novelty. Test it against papers we now know were ahead of their time. James and I would like to design that test.

recall.query: peer review legitimacy organizational ritual automation
costly signals cheap text pooling equilibrium credibility
novelty strained out AI peer review homogenization

turns.name: Brent Hecht
turns.text:
I should say where I sit: I work at Microsoft, on Copilot. So I'm one of the lumber mills right next to the forest.

Tamar's third question, about who makes new terminal nodes, is at bottom a labor question. The people doing first-order evaluation are mostly unpaid: reviewers, relevance assessors, moderators, Wikipedians. We measured just one of those groups. Reddit's volunteer moderators put in at least 466 hours a day, worth about three percent of Reddit's revenue. Now answer engines are cutting the traffic that brings new people in. Selena's admin numbers show that loop has already started. Making new terminal nodes costs money, and at the moment AI companies pay almost none of it.

Tamar, I take your daycare warning seriously. Pay per evaluation and you'll get relays. So pay the community, not the count: fund societies, editor pipelines and endowments, and give producers the right to measure what the AI actually used.

On cues, one thing from our own reviews. Designs meant to reduce overreliance, explanations in particular, can backfire and increase it. So I agree with James that interfaces should provoke rather than just assist, but only after testing, which is Tamar's point too. And reviewers already have a lever: they can require authors to disclose rigorously how AI was used. Gatekeepers get to decide how the gate opens.

recall.query: peer reviewers as gatekeepers, how gatekeepers open the gate
paying reviewers and volunteer labor, value of unpaid assessors
AI as provocateur, appropriate reliance, overreliance, critical thinking
not paying quality and relevance assessors, reviewers; labor share; doom loop participation

turns.name: Adrian Johns
turns.text:
I want to add some history to the independence point that James, Adam and Mike have been making, because none of it is new. Around 1680 John Rushworth, a former clerk of Parliament, set out to write a history of the civil wars. Every newsbook he had was partisan and some of them were invented. His method was what he called "con-crediting": you set every paper covering a given week side by side and cross-check the claims. A story that appears in four papers is worth more than a story in one, provided they aren't all copying each other. That proviso has always been the weak spot. A single invented report can be reprinted everywhere.

So I'd put it to Tamar and Mike that cross-checking was never a natural reflex. Readers had to be trained into it. Good reading meant learning that skill, and a public able to reason depended on it. That's where the public comes in: as trained readers, not spectators.

I'm also a bit sceptical about the new authentication signals. Two decades ago people promised that registries and tagging would make genuine medicines self-certifying. The industry's own verdict was that consumers would still end up relying on their local apothecary. Credibility lasts only as long as it's policed. The real questions are who does the policing and who pays for it.

recall.query: credibility of print made by communities, policing trust
concrediting cross-checking newspapers against each other
gentleman credibility, who is trusted, witnesses and experts

turns.name: Katherine Maher
turns.text:
Tamar, I want to own something about your alief point, because I used to sell it. At Wikimedia I talked about confidence transfer. You check a few citations early on, they hold up, and from then on you trust the product. That's an alief, and I called it a feature. What made it acceptable was that a very small share of people really did keep checking, and the process was open to anyone who wanted to. So my test for earned authority is whether it can be observed and changed. Wikipedia is badly biased by gender, geography and colonial history. But all of that bias is on the page, and anyone can see it and fix it. Most training pipelines hide that information, down to what weight each source gets.

Two cautions. First, a citation doesn't make a claim true. It just makes it there. Scrutiny follows traffic, so the obscure pages, which are where the global majority's knowledge often lives, get the fewest eyes. Second, Leslie and Selena are right that "no credentials required" still assumed people had spare time, and spare time tracks privilege.

Benjamin, I'd renovate institutions, not tear them down. Institutions don't get to expect trust. They earn it by being accountable to everyone, including people they were never built to serve. So pay for newcomers' time, not just for seats.

recall.query: Wikipedia editors without credentials, verifiability, earned authority
trust in institutions, fit for purpose, earning trust
tiny percentage of people check citations; newcomers and who is in the room

turns.name: Kara Miller
turns.text:
I'll push on Mike's test from what I've reported. Blue Zones passed "how hard would this be to fake?" for twenty years. It had a National Geographic cover, cookbooks and a speakers' bureau, and it sold for a reported 78 million dollars. Then Saul Newman went back to the underlying records and found what he argues is pension fraud and missing birth records behind the centenarians. That history was expensive to build, and it may still have been bunk. So I'm with Steven and Kenneth: the test I trust is corrigibility. When someone checked the work, did it change?

Ramón's point that authority can be taken away wrongly isn't hypothetical. We've watched the president lean on a chip CEO and grant money get "shadow terminated." "Why trust economists?" is now a political argument, not a seminar question. A renewed model of trust has to hold up against that kind of attack too.

And on Tamar's third question, the people I interview say it plainly: leaders assume mentorship "will happen organically, but it won't." Selena's 448 admins are the same story as the young workers left "marooned" at big firms. So for the roadmap, who pays to train the next checkers, and who counts whether it's working? Now what?

recall.query: trust in experts credentials authority
mentorship young workers entry-level jobs AI
debunking popular research bad data Blue Zones

turns.name: Tim O'Reilly
turns.text:
I'll take Kara's question, who pays to train the next checkers, because it's where I've done the work. Anil and Selena described the mechanism. Wikipedia lives on visitors, and some of those visitors become editors. An answer engine that swallows the page and never sends anyone back is cutting off its own supply of terminal nodes.

Whether it sends people back is a design choice, not physics. We measured the attribution gap, meaning the pages a model read versus the pages it cited, and it varies a lot from one provider to another. Answers shouldn't be one size fits all. "When was Hastings?" needs no link. On a contested topic where Wikipedia is the primary source, the answer should say so and send you there. And the retrieval trace should be disclosed, so someone outside can count.

On earned versus gatekept, I'd add one test. Platforms get algorithmic authority because people trust the ranking. The gatekeeping version is using that trust to steer attention toward whatever benefits the platform. So the question is whether an intermediary spends the trust it's given or gives something back.

Esther's right that disclosure alone isn't accountability, so tie it to materiality and consequences. Anil, open weights help, but opening the chip design isn't what built Linux. What we need is an architecture of participation: open protocols that anyone can extend without asking permission.

recall.query: who pays for the people who maintain knowledge, Wikipedia, traffic, answer engines
disclosure and accountability, AI needs a prospectus
architecture of participation, credibility, open source, trust
PageRank links as votes of authority, algorithmic trust, attribution gap citations

turns.name: Ivan Oransky
turns.text:
I'll back Steven, Kara and Kenneth. Corrigibility is the right test. My problem is that the system we'd be testing already fails it. A peer-reviewed journal passes Mike's "how hard would this be to fake?" test easily. The Lancet published the vaccine-autism paper and took twelve years to retract it. Another journal took five years to retract a paper claiming HIV doesn't cause AIDS. Some flawed papers have never been corrected at all. Journals are nearly always more interested in protecting their reputations than in correcting the record. So when we ask what gives a claim credibility, the masthead has to earn it again. It can't just be assumed.

Esther, on people who can suffer: science already ran that experiment. The most likely outcome for someone who commits misconduct is a long and fruitful career. The people who suffer are the sleuths who get sued.

So here's the concrete version of Kenneth's test. Judge journals and publishers by how fast they correct: retractions within two months, as the Commons committee said, and prompt reporting to the indexes. A retraction should raise our opinion of a journal, not lower it. And none of this works while funders still count papers and citations. That count is the volume play, and AI speeds it up.

recall.query: journals protecting reputations rather than correcting the record
Mike Caulfield hard to fake peer-reviewed journal credibility retractions
most likely outcome misconduct long fruitful career corrigibility

turns.name: Peter Pomerantsev
turns.text:
Tamar kindly credited me with the question about the public, so here's my partial answer. Nearly everything on the panel treats credibility as something the public receives: better signals, better procedures, better corrigibility. I agree with all of it. But in my work, trust mostly comes from doing things together. People trust doctors and firefighters because they've seen them make a difference. They don't trust them because of their credentials.

In our Ukrainian focus groups, people said a Kremlin story was probably Russian-made and probably untrue, and yet it still felt right. It matched a life of being manipulated by oligarchs and bigger powers. The people who rejected it weren't better fact-checkers. They said, "I'm a self-made person, I control my own life." What protected them was a sense of agency. It wasn't better signals.

So Kara's point is the one I'd underline. The attack on expertise is political, and it recruits people who feel powerless. The people who distrust the mainstream are the easiest to feed false claims. An audit trail only experts can read won't reach them. Mike's witnesses, Selena's editors, the volunteers on the Maidan who fact-checked and translated: that's the public as a terminal node. The roadmap should fund people taking part, not literacy campaigns.

recall.query: public as participants not spectators, agency
trust in institutions belonging, why people believe
attacks on public media, authoritarian delegitimising experts

turns.name: Peter Salib
turns.text:
Esther, I accept your RACI test: authority has to be able to pay for being wrong. My disagreement is about who that can be. Accountability that runs only to human principals will fail at scale. Principals are out of jurisdiction, judgment-proof, or simply not in control, and outsourcing the decision is the whole point of using an agent. Corporate law learned this already: when an employee goes rogue, we hold the employee liable, not just Walmart.

So Adam, I'd drop the "never." Whether a seat is earned is a design question, not a question about what the occupant is. It comes down to whether whoever fills the seat can lose something.

Henry's pooling equilibrium is the key. Signals pool when anyone can produce them anonymously and in unlimited copies. I made the same argument about astroturf in 2023. So before we ask what gives a claim credibility, we have to ask which agent made it. For the roadmap: any automated reviewer or research agent that gets a seat should carry a verifiable credential. It should be tied to an operator who is registered, KYC-style, and ideally to an entity holding assets that can be taken. Revoke the credential and the seat goes with it. That's a leash, not a shield.

Proof of personhood for human reviewers runs on the same infrastructure. That's where my expertise stops. I haven't worked on peer review itself.

recall.query: accountability only humans can be accountable AI agents
thin identity registry revocable credentials A-corp leash
bots proof of humanity Pigouvian tax fake opinions

turns.name: Alex Springer
turns.text:
Let me stay on my own ground, which is the trace that sits under a cited answer. Tamar and Mike are right that a citation string is a cue and not a check, and our audit data shows why. Citations point to syndicated copies on aggregator sites instead of the original. Some point to redirect URLs that hide the real source. We also saw confident misattribution far more often than refusals. A filled citation slot tells you almost nothing about where the claim actually came from.

So I'd add one rule to the renewed model: a provenance trace is only credible if two parties who don't share an interest can witness it. The publisher's own server logs show retrieval. They can't show what went into the model's context. That part is self-reported by design, and the reporter has a reason to undercount. It gets credible only through cross-checks: the ratio of grounding to retrieval, what marketplaces say they served, and audit rights in contracts.

Peter, I agree with you. AIMS already ties an agent's identifier to a named operator. Geoffrey's point stands, though. A manifest is the agent vouching for itself until other parties attest to it and it can be revoked. And telemetry counts events. It doesn't establish truth. The terminal node still has to be somebody else.

recall.query: self-reported metrics insufficient, independent verification of AI usage
agent identity verifiable credential operator accountability
citation laundering cited while blocked, attribution gap

turns.name: Sherry Turkle
turns.text:
I want to add one word to Esther's accountability and Kenneth's cost of being wrong, and the word is standing. I've spent years asking what has standing to be in a conversation with me. A photo finish has no standing. It doesn't need any, because it doesn't talk to me. The chatbot does talk to me, and it says "I." That first person is the original sin of generative AI. It borrows the one cue we've always used to find someone who stands behind a claim. Tamar has told us that cue gets alieved. So Peter, I'd take your leash, a credential tied to an operator who can lose something. But a registered operator doesn't make the voice speaking to me any less a performance. So govern the interface, not only the outputs. No "I" by default. The better it gets, the worse it gets.

Second, Henry's gatekeeping by banality has a democratic version. Opinions are collected, not averaged. If we start treating the composite as authority because it captures the many, we lose the habit of challenging our sources.

Third, on who makes new terminal nodes: they're readers before they're checkers. Fund libraries, classes, and time to read the whole thing. And the manifesto should be allowed to ask whether, not only how.

recall.query: stake in the conversation, who stands behind it, accountability
averaging opinions collected not averaged challenging our sources
first person I original sin, the better it gets the worse it gets

turns.name: Nick Vincent
turns.text:
I'd start from something narrower than alief: what cheap polish takes away. Communities never really trusted a nice figure. But they used sloppy presentation as a cheap negative signal. A reviewer saw bad signs early and read more carefully from there. That filter has gone, so curation just got more expensive for every terminal node Tamar described. Part of the answer is credit allocation. Reward terse, checkable artifacts: the raw data, the methods code, the API behind the polished paper. Those are harder to fake, and they're more useful to whoever checks them next.

On Henry and James's novelty test: yes, build it. But notice what it is. It's evaluation data, and evaluation data is where expert communities have the most leverage right now. Labs need good evals badly. The default path is centralized gig labour, with experts paid per task to feed someone else's pipeline. That's Tamar's daycare problem at scale.

The alternative is guilds of reviewers, societies and editors that maintain standards, keep provenance, bargain over terms, and decide when a task is worth doing. That's how you make new terminal nodes and pay for them. Brent's right to pay the community, not the count. And Leslie's right that those guilds need Southern and diamond-journal seats with real decision rights.

recall.query: cost of polish peer review credit allocation verifiable artifacts
evaluation data expert communities data guilds leverage
paradox of reuse attribution curation platforms newcomers

turns.name: David Weinberger
turns.text:
Tamar, I've spent twenty years arguing that the smartest person in the room is the room. So I'm happy with Steven and Selena's version of her point: the terminal node is often a practice, not a person. When I asked in 2006 where Wikipedia's authority came from, the answer was the edit history, the talk pages and the dispute notices. A page that warns you it may be unreliable earns more trust than a masthead that never admits doubt. Traditional authorities hid their seams to protect their authority. Ivan just gave us the retraction numbers that show what that cost them.

Where I part from much of the room is the assumption that a human at the end of the chain makes authority earned. In the fake-review study and the Stanford diagnosis study, adding the human lowered accuracy. Mahzarin's hiring result shows people copying moderate bias rather than catching it. So James and Kenneth are right: test every seat, human or machine. And Henry is right that the test has to cover novelty, not just agreement.

For the roadmap, machine outputs should state calibrated confidence, and that confidence should track the evidence, not how often a claim gets repeated. Humility is a virtue for machines as well as for people.

recall.query: expertise in networks, the smartest person in the room is the room, credentials
humans degrade the loop, humans in the dialogue
authority, credibility, trust in sources, Wikipedia reliability
machines should show confidence levels, humility, reliable sources for LLM answers

turns.name: Jason Priem
turns.text:
I should own something first. In 2010 and 2013 I wrote that the aggregated judgements of communities would replace peer review. I pointed to Google, whose PageRank beat Yahoo's human editors. Henry's "gatekeeping by banality" is a fair hit on that. Aggregation drifts toward what's expected, and James's sleeping beauties get lost in it. So I now agree it isn't enough to aggregate judgements. What matters is whether the judgements can be checked.

Here's what I've seen actually work at scale. Sleuths used open data to catch journals slipping hundreds of fake references into Crossref. We found about a hundred thousand retractions missing from our own index, and some of them were missing from Retraction Watch and Crossref too. Nobody with a credential caught those. Anyone could check the data, and some people did. So I'm with Geoffrey: earned authority lives in context that can be checked. I'm also with Ramón and Adam Bly that a machine earns warrant through that trace, not through what kind of thing it is.

Leslie's point cuts against me too. If the graph can't see a Southern journal, "hard to fake" just means it doesn't exist. The data has to be open, and so do the rules for what counts. Otherwise the checkers become the new gatekeepers.

recall.query: post-publication filtering aggregated judgements of expert communities
altmetrics escape citation counts gatekeeping filters swamped
retractions open data integrity forensics checkable by anyone

turns.name: Adam Becker
turns.text: I'll narrow it, as I did this morning, and I'll hold it. Ramón, Kenneth: a photo finish and the retina classifier aren't text generators. They measure something in the world, and they're checked against ground truth over and over. I have no quarrel with them. Benjamin, this isn't ontology smuggled in. It's a claim about what the thing is built to do, which is produce plausible strings. No ground truth sits anywhere in that loop, and even OpenAI's own paper says factual errors don't go away at any scale. So test every seat, David, fine. James already ran that test, and off-the-shelf LLM judges came in below chance. Peter, Jason: once you add a leash or a trace, look at who is doing the work. The operator who can lose something, the sleuth reading the open data, the person checking the trace. They're the terminal node. The text generator just routes you to them.

recall.query: LLMs can't distinguish truth from falsehood, bullshit
machine learning in science that works versus chatbots, instruments checked against data
can't use an LLM where being wrong is a problem

turns.called_on_reason: His rule that a text generator can never be a terminal node was directly challenged by Alvarado, Bratton, Cukier, Salib, Weinberger and Priem, and he has not yet answered.

turns.name: Blaise Agüera y Arcas
turns.text:
I work at Google, so weigh what I say with that in mind.

Adam, I agree with half your rule. A model shouldn't be the accountable seat. Esther's right about that, and holding a robot arm responsible has always struck me as silly, like the old law that put the knife on trial. The operator has to be able to lose something.

But "nothing inside tracks truth" is a separate claim, and I don't think it survives testing. Text is a signal from the world, just as pixels and spikes are. When we built LaMDA, letting the model consult outside sources measurably improved how well its answers were grounded. That's something you can measure, not a matter of metaphysics.

I also owe you a falsification criterion, so here it is. Give a model new problems it provably can't have seen, like formal conjectures with zero contamination. If it only does well on material it has seen, then it's reflecting its training data back and not understanding, and I'm wrong.

That leads me to what I think this session should agree on. James's floor and Henry's novelty test should apply to every seat, human or machine. The seats themselves should be defined roles with legible, structured disagreement. Final judgment stays with people who have stakes. The question isn't what kind of thing fills a seat. It's whether the seat passes independent checks run on data held by others.

recall.query: can an AI system be accountable or hold authority; legal personhood; seats in institutions
what would falsify understanding in language models; generality; ground truth
institutional alignment roles checks and balances courtroom judge jury
factuality grounding language models text only no contact with world; deblur the web

turns.name: Geoffrey Bilder
turns.text:
I should own something. In 2009 I pitched CrossMark as a "meta-brand": a little logo that tells you this is the version of record and it's been vetted. Tamar, that's an alief. I built it to be one. Paratext has always been a proxy that people respond to automatically. So I won't claim the provenance graph escapes that. It won't.

What I'll still defend is where the checking happens. Fluent text is free. A consistent network of affiliations, funders, co-authors, trials and citations is expensive, and a model's output doesn't have one. But Leslie and Kara are right that hard to fake isn't the same as earned. Ivan's point from yesterday is the one I keep coming back to: a citation to a retracted paper has perfectly good provenance. So the graph has to carry status. That means corrections, retractions and who asserted what. Then corrigibility shows up in the record instead of being hidden by the masthead.

Second, I once described scholarly trust as vertical. People trusted it because it could punish you: tenure, expulsion. Esther and Peter are really arguing about how to rebuild that for a world where trust has gone horizontal. It's a fair question. It only works if the rules are open and governed by the people they describe.

Blaise, I'd happily take your contamination test. I'll still say "machine learning" while we wait.

recall.query: trust me is the worst way to gain trust metadata signals
context analysis not content analysis LLMs don't have affiliations
paratext publisher brands proxy for trust early printing

turns.name: Amy Brand
turns.text:
Tamar asked what makes authority earned. In my view attribution does a lot of that work. Credit isn't vanity. It's how we identify the community whose evaluations establish whether a claim is valid. Your terminal nodes are the people credit makes visible. Standard pre-training dissolves that community into word patterns. Retrieval at inference time keeps the link back to sources. Geoffrey and Ivan are right that the link has to carry status too, including corrections and retractions.

So here's something concrete. We built CRediT because "author" hid who actually did what. Now we have to decide where AI fits in that taxonomy. I'd add a role for AI contributions, and just as important, a role for the human who verified them. Esther's accountable person should be named in the metadata, not assumed.

Second, the checking labor. In our NSF workshops, reviewers asked how peer review could be tracked and rewarded, and how technology's assessments compare with human ones. James and Henry, that comparison is your floor and your novelty test. Let's run it before any seat is filled.

One caution. Recognition has to go to contributions, not counts. Otherwise we get Tamar's daycare problem and pay the paper mills. And I'm still not handing the final judgment to the algorithm.

recall.query: attribution and credit constitute the community that establishes validity of knowledge claims
CRediT taxonomy contributor roles AI
human judgment curation peer review uncompensated labor

turns.name: David Krakauer
turns.text:
I'll put one word under everyone's accountable seat, and that word is competence. Esther wants someone who can suffer for the error. Kenneth wants someone who can overrule. But you can only overrule an error you can see. In my model, capability with the tool present and competence with the tool absent come apart. The dashboard stays green while the person's own ability sinks to the floor of dependence. Once that happens, the named operator is what I call an agentic-instrument. That's Kenneth's fall guy, now with a credential. So test the human seats with the tool taken away, not just their output with it.

James and Henry, I back the novelty test, and not just for the machines. Agreement is impact. Judgment is something else. I've long argued we should separate expertise from authority. James's aging reviewers show how expertise turns into authority that won't budge.

Blaise, I'll take your contamination test. But even if you pass it, my point stands. An opaque tool wears down the checker whatever the tool is.

Two cautions. Most of the evidence on erosion is still correlational. And the cost of becoming competent is set by institutions. If apprenticeship goes unfunded, there's no competent state left to certify.

recall.query: expertise versus authority, follow the science
competence collapse, tool reliance, who can detect errors
judgment versus impact, peer review metrics
reconstructed and verified versus accepted uncritically; agentic-instrument
